summary: For ages 5–6 (roughly UK Year 1 into early Year 2; US Kindergarten–Grade 1, noting that US standards formally introduce arrays in Grade 2, ages 7–8), use rectangular arrays (equal rows and columns) as a central model for multiplication and division. Learners build arrays, read them two ways to see commutativity, read them as repeated addition, and cover part to reveal division — so one picture yields a whole fact family and seeds the later area model.
misconceptions: Confusing rows with columns and so mis-describing the array (though the total is the same, the language matters for later).
Counting every object one-by-one instead of using the row/column structure (missing the point of the array).
Not seeing that a rotated array has the same total — treating 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts.
Building arrays with unequal rows (ragged rectangles) — breaking the equal-groups structure.
Not recognising the array as a division picture as well as a multiplication one.

activities.title: Build and read an array
steps: Lay out counters (or draw dots) in equal rows and columns to make an array, e.g. 3 rows of 4.
Say aloud exactly what you made: '3 rows of 4' — then also read it as columns: '4 columns of 3'.
Find the total WITHOUT counting every object: skip-count each row, '4, 8, 12'.
Write the multiplication the array shows: 3 × 4 = 12.
Try building another array to order as an extension, e.g. 'Show me 2 × 5 as an array', and state its total.
activities.insight: An array has a regular row/column structure, so you can find the total by using the rows rather than counting every object one by one.

activities.title: Rotate the array to see commutativity
steps: Build 3 rows of 4 and record the total (12).
Turn the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3.
Count or check the total again and notice it is still 12.
Write both multiplications from the one array: 3 × 4 = 12 and 4 × 3 = 12.
activities.insight: Rotating an array turns 3 rows of 4 into 4 rows of 3 while the total stays the same — so 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 is something you can see, not just a rule to remember.

activities.title: Find the division in the same array
steps: Start from a total, e.g. 12 loose counters.
Arrange them into an array with rows of 4; count how many rows you made.
State the division the array shows: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 (12 grouped into rows of 4 makes 3 rows).
Cover the array, tell a partner the total (12) and the number of rows (3), and ask how many are in each row (12 ÷ 3 = 4); then uncover to check.
activities.insight: One array is a division picture as well as a multiplication picture: the rows and columns are the two factors, and reading the total the other way reveals the inverse fact.

activities.title: Write the whole fact family from one array
steps: Look at a single array (e.g. 3 rows of 4).
Also write the array as repeated addition, row by row: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
activities.insight: A single array ties together repeated addition, two multiplication facts and two division facts — it is a key, highly reusable representation, and the same rectangle later becomes the area model for written multiplication.

checkQuestion: Here is an array — 3 rows with 4 counters in each row. Tell me a multiplication this array shows and what the total is. Now here are 12 loose counters — arrange them into an array with rows of 4, and tell me how many rows you made.
checkAnswer: The array shows 3 × 4 = 12 (3 rows of 4). Arranging 12 into rows of 4 makes 3 rows — that same picture shows 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The rows and columns match the two factors.
